title: Evaluate an extension programme in a simple setting

lessons.title: Purpose and planning of an evaluation
lessons.html:
Why evaluate an extension programme?

Evaluation is a systematic look at a programme to judge whether it achieved its objectives, how well it was run, and what should change. A simple setting means one programme with a clear target group, for example a broiler production course for a youth cooperative, or a fodder conservation programme for twenty communal livestock owners in one ward.

Evaluation serves several purposes:

  • Accountability: showing funders, the department or the community how resources were used.
  • Learning: finding out what worked and what did not, so the next programme is better.
  • Decision-making: deciding whether to continue, expand, change or stop the programme.

Monitoring and evaluation are different

Monitoring is the routine tracking of activities during the programme: sessions held, attendance, inputs delivered, money spent. Evaluation uses monitoring data plus extra information to make a judgement, usually at mid-term and at the end.

Planning the evaluation

  1. Go back to the programme plan and list its objectives. Good objectives are specific and measurable, for example: by the end of the season, 15 of the 20 members will have made and stored silage.
  2. Write evaluation questions. Did members learn to make silage? How many actually made it? Did winter weight losses fall? Were members satisfied with the training?
  3. Decide on indicators for each question.
  4. Choose who will provide information: participants, family members, lead farmers, partners and your own records.
  5. Set a timeline and budget, even if small.

Baseline information

To show change you need a starting point. Ideally, information such as herd numbers, typical winter losses or current practices was collected before the programme began. If no baseline exists, you can ask participants to recall the situation before, but treat this information with care because memory is not always accurate.

lessons.title: Collecting and analysing evaluation information
lessons.html:
Gathering the evidence

In a simple setting, use a mix of practical methods. Combining numbers with farmers' own stories gives a fuller picture.

MethodUse it for
Short questionnaireKnowledge, practices and satisfaction across all participants
Farm visits and observationChecking whether practices are actually used
Focus group discussionUnderstanding reasons, problems and suggestions
RecordsAttendance, yields, sales, mortalities, costs
Key informant interviewsViews of lead farmers, partners or traditional leaders

Good practice in data collection

  • Explain the purpose of the evaluation and get consent. Participation must be voluntary.
  • Keep questions short and clear, and translate them into the local language.
  • Avoid leading questions such as: You found the training very useful, didn't you?
  • Allow farmers to give negative feedback without fear of losing support.
  • Keep personal information confidential.

Analysing the information

For numbers, use simple counts, percentages and averages. For example: 14 of 20 members (70 percent) made silage, compared with the target of 15. Average winter weight loss fell from an estimated 40 kg to 25 kg per animal according to members' weighband records.

For discussions and interviews, group comments into themes, such as lack of chopping equipment, late delivery of plastic, or strong support from the lead farmer. Count how often each theme comes up.

Judging results fairly

Ask whether the programme caused the change or whether other factors played a part, such as a good rainy season or a separate government feed scheme. Be honest about this. Also look for unexpected results, both positive and negative, such as members starting to sell silage to neighbours.

lessons.title: Reporting and using evaluation findings
lessons.html:
Turning findings into action

An evaluation only has value when its findings are shared and used. Write a short, clear report and present it to the people who need it.

Structure of a simple evaluation report

  1. Summary: one page with the main findings and recommendations.
  2. Background: programme objectives, target group, area and dates.
  3. Method: how information was collected, from whom and any limitations.
  4. Findings: results for each evaluation question, with numbers and quotes.
  5. Conclusions: did the programme meet its objectives, and why or why not.
  6. Recommendations: practical, specific actions, each with a responsible person.

Reporting to different audiences

  • Supervisor or funder: the written report with figures and costs.
  • Participants and community: a report-back meeting in the local language using simple charts or a flip chart, so farmers see what their information showed.
  • Partners: a short summary of what their contribution achieved.

Writing useful recommendations

Weak recommendation: improve the programme. Strong recommendation: arrange a shared chaff cutter through the cooperative before the next silage season, led by the cooperative chairperson with support from the extension officer.

Ethics and honesty

Report what you found, even when results are disappointing. Inflating figures to please a funder damages trust and leads to poor decisions. State the limitations of your evaluation, such as a small sample or missing baseline data.

Closing the loop

Use the recommendations when planning the next programme cycle, and check later whether they were carried out. This turns evaluation into continuous improvement.

Key points

  • Evaluation judges whether objectives were achieved and what to improve.
  • Start from measurable objectives, evaluation questions and indicators.
  • Combine records, observation, questionnaires and discussions.
  • Consider other factors that may explain results.
  • Report honestly to all audiences, including the participants.
